blocks.text: In a nuclear power station the reactor plays the same part as the furnace in a thermal power station: in a furnace coal or oil is burnt to produce heat, while in a reactor fission produces heat. Fission of a uranium (or other heavy) nucleus releases about 200 MeV, appearing as kinetic energy of the fission fragments. These fast fragments collide with one another and with uranium atoms, and their kinetic energy becomes heat. The heat makes steam, which turns a turbine, which turns a generator that produces electricity (Fig 19.5).

blocks.alt: Inside a concrete shield: a steel pressure vessel holding red fuel elements, black control rods and water at high pressure. Hot water leaves the top right of the vessel past the pressurizer to the heat exchanger, flows down through its coiled pipe and returns through the pump to the vessel (green arrows). Two pipes leave the heat exchanger through the shield: the upper one outwards (red arrow), the lower one inwards (blue arrow).

items: Core: the most important part of the reactor, where the fuel is kept as cylindrical rods. Uranium was used as fuel in early reactors, with the proportion of uranium-235 enriched to 2.4 to 3.0 per cent; natural uranium contains only 0.7 per cent of it. Plutonium-239 and uranium-233 are also used as fuel.

Moderator: the fuel rods sit in a substance of low atomic mass such as water or heavy water (made with deuterium, 2-1-H, instead of ordinary hydrogen). Its job is to slow down the fast, energetic neutrons produced in fission, because slow neutrons are much more effective at causing fission in fuel such as uranium-235 or plutonium-239.

Control rods: rods of cadmium or boron, which absorb neutrons, are moved in or out of the core so that, of all the neutrons produced in each fission, only one causes a further fission; this keeps the chain reaction under control. In an emergency or for repairs, the rods are dropped fully into the reactor to stop the chain reaction and shut it down.

Coolant and heat exchanger: the core temperature rises to about 500 C. The heat is carried to a heat exchanger by water, heavy water or another liquid under high pressure, where it turns ordinary water into high-temperature steam that drives the turbine and generator. The steam leaving the turbine, at about 300 C, is cooled back into water, generally with water from a river or the sea.
Shielding and safety: the whole reactor is enclosed in a thick concrete shield to stop radiation escaping.

blocks.alt: A neutron (1-0-n) plus 238-92-U gives 239-92-U plus gamma. After 23.5 min, 239-92-U becomes 239-93-Np plus an electron (0-(-1)-e) plus gamma. After 2.4 days, 239-93-Np becomes 239-94-Pu plus an electron plus gamma.
blocks.caption: Do you know? box: An induced nuclear reaction in which 238-92-U is transmuted into the transuranium element plutonium 239-94-Pu (original drawing after the textbook's Do you know? box).

blocks.text: At the Karachi nuclear power plant (KANUPP), heavy water is used both as the moderator and to carry heat from the core to the heat exchanger, while sea water cools the steam from the turbine. Three nuclear power plants operate in Karachi and four at Chashma (Mianwali), with a total capacity of more than 3000 MW, all pressurised water reactors cooled by water from the nearby Indus river.

Nuclear fuel loaded into a reactor runs it for a few months; then the fissile material begins to run low, the used fuel is removed and fresh fuel is fed in. The used fuel still contains intensely radioactive substances with half-lives of many thousands of years, whose radiation is very harmful to living things. Nuclear waste cannot be dumped into the oceans or left where it could contaminate the soil, air or drinking water. The best place found so far to store it is deep in old salt mines, which are very dry and thousands of metres below the surface, where it can decay without polluting the environment.

blocks.title: Do you know? Radioactive waste
blocks.text: Radioactive wastes are of three types, high level, medium level and low level, and all are dangerous for ground water and the land environment. Safe disposal is very difficult because of long half-lives: plutonium's half-life is about 24,000 years, so it stays dangerous for about 182,000 years. The trefoil radiation symbol marks areas where radioactivity is handled or artificial radiation is produced.
